The parser looks up A2 on the cell master, finds its direction from the library, and attaches an ITerm to n1. The fanout of a net is the number of input pins it drives. In `NAND2_X1 u3 (.A1(n1), .A2(n1), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(n1), .ZN(y0));`, net n1 drives u3/A1, u3/A2 and u4/A: fanout 3, even though only two instances read it, because each pin is a separate sink. Output pins such as ZN are drivers and are not counted. Fanout feeds everything downstream: load capacitance for timing, net weights for placement, and buffering decisions.

## Positional connections need the cell's port order

Verilog also allows positional connections: `NAND2_X1 u5 (n1, b, n3);` binds signals to ports in the order the cell's module declares them. The netlist alone cannot tell you which signal is the output: the parser needs the port order, from a Verilog cell library or from the order the tool assumes for the master. If NAND2_X1 is declared as (A1, A2, ZN), then n1 is A1, b is A2 and n3 is the output ZN. Get the order wrong and the parser silently turns an output into an input, creating a net with two drivers and a dangling sink. Robust readers therefore check that every net has exactly one driver after reading, and treat positional connections to cells without a declared port order as an error. Escaped identifiers such as `\bus[3] ` (a backslash name ended by whitespace) are another trap for hand-written lexers.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1364-2005, the Verilog standard, sections on module instantiation; the Yosys manual on reading and writing netlists; the OpenROAD documentation for read_verilog and link_design.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1); input a, b, c; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2; INV_X1 u1 (.A(b), .ZN(n1)); NAND2_X1 u2 (.A1(c), .A2(c), .ZN(n2)); NOR2_X1 u3 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .ZN(y0)); BUF_X1 u4 (.A(a), .Z(y1)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 3 inputs and 2 outputs, plus 2 declared wires, gives 7 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, y0); input a, b, c; output y0; wire n1, n2, n3; INV_X1 u1 (.A(c), .ZN(n1)); NAND2_X1 u2 (.A1(a), .A2(c), .ZN(n2)); INV_X1 u3 (.A(n1), .ZN(n3)); AND2_X1 u4 (.A1(n2), .A2(n3), .ZN(y0)); endmodule` How many nets does the block contain? Count every distinct signal, ports included.
problems.e: Each port is also a net: 3 inputs and 1 outputs, plus 3 declared wires, gives 7 nets. Every instance drives exactly one net here, so the count is inputs plus instances.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist into a design database: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1); input a, b, c; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2, n3, n4, n5; INV_X1 u1 (.A(a), .ZN(n1)); AOI21_X1 u2 (.A(b), .B1(c), .B2(a), .ZN(n2)); BUF_X1 u3 (.A(n1), .Z(y0)); NAND3_X1 u4 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .A3(n2), .ZN(n3)); NOR2_X1 u5 (.A1(n1), .A2(n1), .ZN(n4)); INV_X1 u6 (.A(n4), .ZN(n5)); NAND3_X1 u7 (.A1(n3), .A2(n1), .A3(n5), .ZN(y1)); endmodule` How many instance terminals (ITerms) does it create? Count one per pin of every instance, inputs and outputs.
problems.e: One ITerm per instance pin: u1 has 2, u2 has 4, u3 has 2, u4 has 4, u5 has 3, u6 has 2, u7 has 4, for 21 in all. Ports become BTerms, not ITerms.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1); input a, b, c; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2, n3, n4; NAND3_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(a), .A3(b), .ZN(n1)); INV_X1 u2 (.A(a), .ZN(y0)); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(c), .A2(c), .ZN(n2)); NOR2_X1 u4 (.A1(b), .A2(n1), .ZN(n3)); BUF_X1 u5 (.A(n2), .Z(n4)); AOI21_X1 u6 (.A(c), .B1(n4), .B2(n3), .ZN(y1)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n3 drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for n3 and keep the input pins: u6/B2, which is 1.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, y0, y1); input a, b; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2; BUF_X1 u1 (.A(b), .Z(n1)); BUF_X1 u2 (.A(b), .Z(n2)); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(n2), .A2(a), .ZN(y0)); NAND2_X1 u4 (.A1(n2), .A2(n1), .ZN(y1)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net b drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for b and keep the input pins: u1/A and u2/A, which is 2.

problems.q: A parser reads this netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2; NAND2_X1 u1 (.A1(b), .A2(a), .ZN(n1)); BUF_X1 u2 (.A(b), .Z(n2)); AOI21_X1 u3 (.A(n1), .B1(n2), .B2(n2), .ZN(y0)); INV_X1 u4 (.A(c), .ZN(y1)); INV_X1 u5 (.A(n2), .ZN(y2)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n2 drive (its fanout)?
problems.e: Scan every connection for n2 and keep the input pins: u3/B1, u3/B2 and u5/A, which is 3.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders NOR2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); NAND3_X1 (A1, A2, A3, ZN); BUF_X1 (A, Z); INV_X1 (A, ZN). Netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1, y2, y3); input a, b, c; output y0, y1, y2, y3; wire n1; NOR2_X1 u1 (c, a, n1); NOR2_X1 u2 (b, c, y0); NAND3_X1 u3 (b, c, c, y1); BUF_X1 u4 (n1, y2); INV_X1 u5 (.A(c), .ZN(y3)); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net c drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on c are u1/A1, u2/A2, u3/A2, u3/A3 and u5/A, which is 5.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders AOI21_X1 (A, B1, B2, ZN); NAND3_X1 (A1, A2, A3, ZN); AND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); BUF_X1 (A, Z). Netlist: `module top (a, b, c, y0, y1); input a, b, c; output y0, y1; wire n1, n2; AOI21_X1 u1 (.A(a), .B1(a), .B2(b), .ZN(n1)); NAND3_X1 u2 (a, b, c, n2); AND2_X1 u3 (.A1(c), .A2(n2), .ZN(y0)); BUF_X1 u4 (n1, y1); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net a drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on a are u1/A, u1/B1 and u2/A1, which is 3.

problems.q: Some instances below connect by position. The library declares the port orders NAND3_X1 (A1, A2, A3, ZN); AND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); NAND2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); NOR2_X1 (A1, A2, ZN); BUF_X1 (A, Z); INV_X1 (A, ZN). Netlist: `module top (a, b, c, d, y0, y1, y2); input a, b, c, d; output y0, y1, y2; wire n1, n2, n3, n4, n5; NAND3_X1 u1 (.A1(a), .A2(c), .A3(b), .ZN(n1)); AND2_X1 u2 (.A1(d), .A2(c), .ZN(n2)); NAND2_X1 u3 (n2, n2, n3); NOR2_X1 u4 (d, n1, n4); NAND3_X1 u5 (n4, n4, n2, n5); BUF_X1 u6 (.A(n4), .Z(y0)); NAND3_X1 u7 (.A1(n2), .A2(n5), .A3(n3), .ZN(y1)); INV_X1 u8 (n4, y2); endmodule` How many instance input pins does net n2 drive?
problems.e: Map each positional connection onto the declared port order, where the last position is the output pin. The input pins on n2 are u3/A1, u3/A2, u5/A3 and u7/A1, which is 4.

label: Parsing Liberty
lesson:
# Parsing Liberty

Liberty (.lib) files carry the timing, power and function of every library cell, and every synthesis, timing and power tool must read them. The format is a simple nested grammar of groups and attributes, but real libraries are huge and full of vendor extensions. A tool designer must parse the grammar generically, interpret the timing semantics correctly, and do both fast enough for files of hundreds of megabytes.

## Groups, simple and complex attributes

Liberty has three statement shapes. A group has a name, a parenthesized argument and a braced body: `cell (NAND2_X1) { ... }`, `pin (A1) { ... }`, `timing () { ... }`. A simple attribute is `name : value ;`, for example `direction : input ;` or `time_unit : "1ns" ;`. A complex attribute is `name (v1, v2, ...) ;`, for example `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` or `index_1 ("0.01, 0.04, 0.16") ;`. Because every statement has one of these three shapes whatever its name, one small recursive-descent parser can build a generic tree of groups and attributes for any Liberty file, including vendor attributes it has never seen. A second pass interprets the tree into cells, pins and arcs. This split keeps the grammar code tiny and puts all the semantics in one place.

## What the parser must keep for timing

Timing lives in `timing ()` groups inside the pin where the arc ends. For the arc from A1 to ZN of a NAND2, the group sits inside `pin (ZN)` with `related_pin : "A1"` and `timing_sense : negative_unate`. Inside it, tables such as `cell_rise (delay_template_7x7)` and `rise_transition (...)` hold `index_1`, `index_2` and `values`. The template name points to an `lu_table_template` declared earlier at library level, whose `variable_1` and `variable_2` say which axis is input transition and which is output load. The parser must keep the template binding, both index vectors, the value matrix (checking it has as many rows as index_1 entries and columns as index_2 entries), the related pin, the timing sense and any `when` condition. The output pin's `function` string, such as `"!(A1 & A2)"`, gives the logic that synthesis needs.

## Scale, streaming and the header

A library for one process corner can run to hundreds of megabytes, almost all of it tables. A placer needs only areas and pin capacitances; a timer needs the tables but maybe not the power data. A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the rest, while still tracking brace nesting, saves both time and memory. Order matters: units such as `time_unit` and `capacitive_load_unit` and the table templates are declared in the library header before the cells, so a parser can convert values as it reads them. A table that names an undeclared template is an error, not something to guess at. Several libraries in one session can use different units, so conversion into the tool's internal units must happen per library at read time. Error messages need file and line numbers, since users fix libraries by hand.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual (the open Liberty specification); the OpenSTA source for its Liberty reader; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter on cell libraries.

problems.q:
A Liberty parser meets `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` in the library header. Which construct is it?

A) A complex attribute: a name with a parenthesized value list

B) A simple attribute: a name, a colon and one value

C) A define statement that declares a new attribute

D) A group: a name, arguments and a braced body
problems.a: A complex attribute: a name with a parenthesized value list
problems.e: Liberty has three statement shapes. Simple attributes use `name : value ;`, complex attributes use `name (v1, v2, ...) ;`, and groups add a braced body.

problems.q:
A generic Liberty parser builds a tree from the grammar alone, before knowing what `cell_rise` means. What does the tree contain?

A) A flat table of every timing arc in the library

B) Only the cells, with the header attributes discarded

C) Nested groups, each with its arguments, attributes and child groups

D) A delay-calculation graph with arcs between pins
problems.a: Nested groups, each with its arguments, attributes and child groups
problems.e: Liberty's syntax is uniform, so a first pass can build a generic tree of groups and attributes; a second pass interprets it into cells, pins and arcs.

problems.q:
Why can one grammar parse every Liberty file even though vendors add their own attributes?

A) The grammar lists every legal attribute name explicitly

B) Unknown attributes are rejected, so files only use standard names

C) Every statement is a group, a simple attribute or a complex attribute, whatever its name

D) Vendors must register each attribute with the parser at build time
problems.a: Every statement is a group, a simple attribute or a complex attribute, whatever its name
problems.e: The syntax does not depend on the attribute vocabulary. A parser can keep or skip unknown names and still recover the structure.

problems.q:
A `cell_rise (delay_template_7x7)` group has index_1, index_2 and values. What must the parser resolve to interpret the indices?

A) The default_max_transition of the library

B) The cell's area attribute

C) The lu_table_template named delay_template_7x7, which says which variable each index is

D) The related_pin of the next timing group
problems.a: The lu_table_template named delay_template_7x7, which says which variable each index is
problems.e: The template declares variable_1 and variable_2, for example input transition and output load, so the parser knows which axis is which and can fall back to its default indices.

problems.q:
Which pin attribute lets a logic tool recover what a cell computes?

A) `direction : output` on the output pin

B) `related_pin : "A1"` in the timing group

C) `function : "!(A1 & A2)"` on the output pin

D) `area : 0.798` on the cell
problems.a: `function : "!(A1 & A2)"` on the output pin
problems.e: The function string is a Boolean expression of the input pins; synthesis and equivalence checkers parse it into logic.

problems.q:
In a Liberty cell, where does the timing group for the arc from input A1 to output ZN live?

A) Directly under the cell, outside any pin

B) Inside pin (ZN), with `related_pin : "A1"`

C) In the library header, keyed by cell name

D) Inside pin (A1), with `related_pin : "ZN"`
problems.a: Inside pin (ZN), with `related_pin : "A1"`
problems.e: Timing groups sit in the pin they arrive at, and related_pin names the pin the arc starts from.

problems.q:
A library for one corner is several hundred megabytes, but a placer needs only pin capacitances and cell areas. What parser design fits best?

A) A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the bodies it does not

B) Converting the file to XML first, then parsing the XML

C) A full in-memory tree of every group, then a query pass

D) Reading only the first megabyte, where the cells are
problems.a: A streaming parser that interprets the groups it needs and skips the bodies it does not
problems.e: Most of the bytes are timing and power tables. Skipping unneeded groups while still tracking brace nesting saves time and memory.

problems.q:
A parser reads `cell_rise (tmpl_A)` before it has seen any lu_table_template named tmpl_A. What should it do?

A) Silently treat the table as scalar

B) Report an error, because templates must be declared before tables refer to them

C) Search the next library file for the template

D) Assume a 7 × 7 template with default indices
problems.a: Report an error, because templates must be declared before tables refer to them
problems.e: Templates are declared at library level before use. Guessing a template would misread the axes and corrupt every delay looked up from that table.

problems.q:
Two libraries are read into one session, one with time_unit "1ns" and one with time_unit "1ps". Where must the scaling happen?

A) Only when a report is printed

B) Never; the timer uses the first library's unit for both

C) When the netlist is linked, from the cell names

D) When each library is read, converting its values into the tool's internal units
problems.a: When each library is read, converting its values into the tool's internal units
problems.e: Units are per library. Converting at read time means every engine downstream sees one consistent unit system.

label: Liberty units and scaling
lesson:
# Liberty units and scaling

Liberty tables are just numbers; their meaning comes from unit attributes in the library header. A delay of 0.05 is 50 ps in one library and 0.05 ps in another. Every reader must scale each value by its library's units into one internal unit system, and every consumer must trust that it did. Unit bugs are silent: the tool runs, and every slack is wrong by a factor of a thousand.

## Time units scale delay tables

The header attribute `time_unit` takes one of the values "1ps", "10ps", "100ps" or "1ns", and every delay and transition value in the library is a multiple of it. With `time_unit : "1ns" ;`, a `cell_rise` entry of 0.0532 is $0.0532 \times 1000 = 53.2$ ps. With "10ps", an entry of 5.32 is also 53.2 ps. The input-transition axis of a table (index_1 in a typical delay template) is in the same time unit. A reader converts at parse time: it computes the factor once from the header, multiplies each value as it stores it, and keeps everything internally in one unit, often seconds as a double, so that engines never see library units at all.

## Capacitive load units scale pins and indices

Capacitance uses the complex attribute `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` or `(1,ff)`. Pin capacitances and the output-load axis of delay tables (often index_2) are multiples of it. A pin with `capacitance : 0.0016 ;` in a pF library is 1.6 fF. The conversion runs both ways. When a timer computes a net load of 4.5 fF and must look it up in a pF table, it needs the index value $4.5 / 1000 = 0.0045$. Doing the lookup with 4.5 instead would land far beyond the table's last index and extrapolate wildly. Libraries also declare `voltage_unit`, `current_unit`, `pulling_resistance_unit` and `leakage_power_unit`, each handled the same way.

## Units belong to each library

A session often loads several libraries: standard cells, IO cells, memories from a generator. Nothing forces them to share units. Suppose library A uses "1ns" and library B uses "1ps", and a path has arc delays 0.12 (A), 35 (B) and 0.08 (A). The path delay is $120 + 35 + 80 = 235$ ps. Adding the raw numbers gives 35.2, which means nothing. This is why scaling belongs in the reader, per library, rather than in the timer: the timer adds delays from many cells and cannot know which library each number came from unless the reader already normalized it. A related trap is SDC: its numbers are unitless and take their meaning from `set_units` or from the library units, so changing libraries can silently change what a constraint means.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, library-level attributes; the OpenSTA source for unit handling in its Liberty reader.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "10ps" ;`. A cell_fall table entry for one arc reads 17.6. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 10ps = 10 ps, so 17.6 × 10 = 176 ps.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "100ps" ;`. A rise_transition table entry for one arc reads 2.733. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 100ps = 100 ps, so 2.733 × 100 = 273.3 ps.

problems.q: A Liberty library header declares `time_unit : "100ps" ;`. A cell_rise table entry for one arc reads 1.882. What is that delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Table values are in the library time unit, 100ps = 100 ps, so 1.882 × 100 = 188.2 ps.

problems.q: A timer must look up an output load of 23.8 fF in a delay table whose index_2 is total_output_net_capacitance. The library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;`. What index_2 value, in library units, corresponds to that load? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: Index values share the load unit, 1000 fF per unit, so 23.8 fF is 0.0238 library units.

problems.q: A timer must look up an output load of 4 fF in a delay table whose index_2 is total_output_net_capacitance. The library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;`. What index_2 value, in library units, corresponds to that load? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: Index values share the load unit, 1000 fF per unit, so 4 fF is 0.004 library units.

problems.q: A Liberty library declares `capacitive_load_unit (1,pf) ;` and an input pin has `capacitance : 0.0027 ;`. What is the pin capacitance in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Capacitance values are in the load unit (1,pf), which is 1000 fF, so the pin is 2.7 fF.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "100ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.268 from library A, 1.74 from library B, 0.157 from library A, 1.97 from library B. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 100, for 796 ps. Adding the raw numbers (4.135) mixes units.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "100ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.172 from library A, 2.25 from library B, 0.214 from library A. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 100, for 611 ps. Adding the raw numbers (2.636) mixes units.

problems.q: A path crosses cells from two libraries. Library A declares `time_unit : "1ns" ;` and library B declares `time_unit : "1ps" ;`. The arc delays read from the tables are 0.275 from library A, 117 from library B, 257 from library B. What is the path delay in ps? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Each value is scaled by its own library's unit before summing: A values × 1000, B values × 1, for 649 ps. Adding the raw numbers (374.275) mixes units.

label: Parsing LEF and DEF
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Parsing LEF and DEF

LEF and DEF are the physical interchange formats of digital implementation. LEF describes the technology and the abstract of each cell; DEF describes one design's floorplan, instances, pins, nets and routing. A design database such as OpenDB follows their structure closely, so reading them is how a physical tool comes to life. A reader must map each section onto database objects and resolve every cross-reference between the two files.

## Technology LEF and cell LEF

LEF comes in two parts. Technology LEF defines units (`DATABASE MICRONS`), the manufacturing grid, routing and cut layers (with DIRECTION, PITCH, WIDTH and SPACING), via definitions and placement SITEs. Cell LEF defines one MACRO per library cell: its CLASS (CORE, PAD, BLOCK...), its SIZE w BY h in microns, the SITE it fits, and its PINs with DIRECTION, USE and PORT shapes on layers. OBS lists internal metal that routes must avoid. LEF is deliberately an abstract: it gives a router the pin access shapes and blockages but not the transistors inside, and it holds no timing. Pin capacitance and delay come from Liberty, which is why a timer needs both files.

## DEF sections and what they build

A DEF begins with VERSION, DESIGN and `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS n`, then DIEAREA. ROW statements create the placement rows from the LEF site, TRACKS the legal routing tracks per layer and GCELLGRID the global-routing tiles. COMPONENTS creates instances: `- u7 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 3800 5600 ) FS ;` gives the master, a status (PLACED, FIXED, UNPLACED) and an orientation (N, S, FN, FS and so on). PINS creates the block's ports with their shapes. NETS gives connectivity as lists of (instance pin) pairs, plus routing once routed; SPECIALNETS carries power straps and rings; BLOCKAGES carries placement and routing blockages. Each section maps onto a database object kind, which is why a DEF reader is a sequence of section handlers.

## Reading order and cross-references

DEF refers to LEF by name: components name masters, ROWs name sites, routing names layers and vias. So LEF must be read first, and every name must resolve. When a NETS entry says `( u7 A3 )` but the master has only A1, A2 and ZN, the reader should report the error with a line number and keep going, never invent a pin. Units must also agree: the DEF resolution may not be finer than the LEF `DATABASE MICRONS`, so a 2000 LEF with a 1000 DEF is fine. Scale matters too. A large DEF can be tens of gigabytes, mostly NETS. The Si2 reference parsers, which OpenDB builds on, are callback-driven: the parser hands each component or net to the database as it is read, instead of building an intermediate tree.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference (distributed with the Si2 LEF/DEF parsers); the OpenDB documentation in OpenROAD; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1.

problems.q:
A PIN in a cell LEF has a PORT with RECT shapes on metal1. What does a parser store for it?

A) The pin's logic function

B) The pin's placement in the die

C) The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin

D) The pin's capacitance for timing
problems.a: The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin
problems.e: LEF describes physical abstraction: shapes and layers. Electrical data such as capacitance comes from Liberty.

problems.q:
A PIN in a cell LEF has a PORT with RECT shapes on metal1. What does a parser store for it?

A) The pin's logic function

B) The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin

C) The pin's capacitance for timing

D) The pin's placement in the die
problems.a: The pin's access geometry, which the router uses to connect wires to the pin
problems.e: LEF describes physical abstraction: shapes and layers. Electrical data such as capacitance comes from Liberty.

problems.q:
A reader finds LAYER metal2 with DIRECTION, PITCH, WIDTH and SPACING statements. Which file is it reading?

A) The DEF NETS section

B) A cell LEF

C) A Liberty library

D) A technology LEF
problems.a: A technology LEF
problems.e: Technology LEF defines the routing layers, vias, sites and units; cell LEF defines MACROs.

problems.q:
A DEF line reads `- u7 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 3800 5600 ) FS ;`. What does FS give the database?

A) The orientation: mirrored about the x-axis, as used for flipped rows

B) The fixed status, meaning the placer must not move it

C) The first site of the row

D) The fill-cell status of the instance
problems.a: The orientation: mirrored about the x-axis, as used for flipped rows
problems.e: N, S, E, W, FN, FS, FE and FW are orientations. FS is the mirror used for flipped rows; FIXED and PLACED are placement statuses.

problems.q:
A DEF has TRACKS and GCELLGRID statements. Which engine relies on them most?

A) The parser, for its unit scaling

B) The timer, for its clock definitions

C) The router, for its routing grid and its global-routing tiles

D) The placer, for its site legality
problems.a: The router, for its routing grid and its global-routing tiles
problems.e: TRACKS define legal wire positions per layer and GCELLGRID the coarse tiles of global routing.

problems.q:
Which DEF section creates the instances of a design?

A) ROWS

B) COMPONENTS

C) PINS

D) NETS
problems.a: COMPONENTS
problems.e: COMPONENTS lists each instance with its master and, when placed, its location and orientation. PINS creates the block's ports.

problems.q:
A reader streams a 20 GB DEF. Which section benefits most from a callback-style parser that hands each entry to the database as it is read?

A) VERSION, which is one token

B) UNITS, which is a single line

C) DIEAREA, which is one rectangle

D) NETS, which carries the connectivity and routing of millions of nets
problems.a: NETS, which carries the connectivity and routing of millions of nets
problems.e: Callback parsers (the Si2 LEF/DEF reference parsers work this way) avoid holding an intermediate copy of the biggest sections.

problems.q:
A DEF NETS entry connects `( u7 A3 )`, but the LEF MACRO for u7's master has only pins A1, A2 and ZN. What should a robust reader do?

A) Report the unknown pin and keep reading, so the user sees every such error

B) Create a new pin A3 on the master

C) Connect the net to A1 instead

D) Drop the whole NETS section
problems.a: Report the unknown pin and keep reading, so the user sees every such error
problems.e: Cross-reference errors are design bugs. Reporting them with line numbers, without inventing pins, is what lets a user fix the input.

problems.q:
A reader streams a 20 GB DEF. Which section benefits most from a callback-style parser that hands each entry to the database as it is read?

A) NETS, which carries the connectivity and routing of millions of nets

B) UNITS, which is a single line

C) DIEAREA, which is one rectangle

D) VERSION, which is one token
problems.a: NETS, which carries the connectivity and routing of millions of nets
problems.e: Callback parsers (the Si2 LEF/DEF reference parsers work this way) avoid holding an intermediate copy of the biggest sections.

label: DEF database units
lesson:
# DEF database units

DEF stores every coordinate as an integer in database units, declared once by `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS n`. Integers make geometry exact and comparisons cheap, but every reader and writer must convert correctly between microns and units, and LEF dimensions arrive in microns. Unit conversion is the first computation any physical-design tool performs, and the source of some of its most confusing bugs.

## From DEF integers to microns

With `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 2000`, one micron is 2000 database units (dbu), so one dbu is 0.5 nm. The component line `- u12 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 38000 57600 ) N ;` puts the instance origin at $x = 38000 / 2000 = 19$ um and $y = 57600 / 2000 = 28.8$ um. The value of n is chosen by the writer from a fixed set (100, 200, 1000, 2000 and so on); it must be no finer than the LEF `DATABASE MICRONS`. Inside a database the integers are usually kept as they are, and conversion to microns happens only for reports and user input, so the engines work in exact integer arithmetic. A coordinate that is not a whole number of database units cannot be written at all, which is why a writer that rescales a design to a coarser resolution must snap every shape and report what moved.

## Die area from DIEAREA

`DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 600000 400000 ) ;` with 2000 units per micron is a die of $600000 / 2000 = 300$ um by $400000 / 2000 = 200$ um, so $300 \times 200 = 60000$ square microns. Area scales with the square of the unit: a product of two dbu lengths is in dbu squared, so the conversion divides by $n^2 = 4{,}000{,}000$, not by n. Dividing once is the classic mistake, and gives an area 2000 times too large. When the lower-left corner is not at the origin, as in `DIEAREA ( 2000 2000 ) ( 602000 402000 )`, subtract corners first. DIEAREA can also be a rectilinear polygon with more points, in which case the area comes from the polygon, not the bounding box.

## LEF microns into DEF rows

LEF gives the SITE width in microns, for example 0.19 um. A DEF row `ROW ROW_0 core 3800 5600 N DO 400 BY 1 STEP 380 0 ;` with 2000 units per micron uses a step of $0.19 \times 2000 = 380$ dbu, and its right edge is at $3800 + 400 \times 380 = 155800$ dbu. Every LEF dimension must land on an integer at the DEF resolution, which is one reason resolutions are chosen to match the manufacturing grid: a 0.005 um grid needs at least 200 units per micron. If a conversion produces a fraction, the writer must round, and a rounded site width accumulates error across hundreds of sites in a row, which breaks legality checks in the placer.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference, sections on UNITS, DIEAREA and ROW; the OpenDB documentation on database units.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 200 ;` and its COMPONENTS section has `- u1594 NOR2_X1 + PLACED ( 168226 40148 ) N ;`. What is the x coordinate of the instance origin in microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: DEF stores integers in database units; one micron is 200 units, so 168226 / 200 = 841.13 microns.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 2000 ;` and its COMPONENTS section has `- u1335 NAND3_X1 + PLACED ( 1229500 128920 ) N ;`. What is the x coordinate of the instance origin in microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: DEF stores integers in database units; one micron is 2000 units, so 1229500 / 2000 = 614.75 microns.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 100 ;` and its COMPONENTS section has `- u6285 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 48757 30612 ) N ;`. What is the x coordinate of the instance origin in microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: DEF stores integers in database units; one micron is 100 units, so 48757 / 100 = 487.57 microns.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 100 ;` and `DIEAREA ( 50 100 ) ( 2060 7220 ) ;`. What is the die area in square microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Width is 2010 dbu = 20.1 um and height 7120 dbu = 71.2 um, so the area is 1431.12 square microns. Dividing the product of dbu by 100 once, not 100 squared, is the classic error.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 ;` and `DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 41700 33800 ) ;`. What is the die area in square microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Width is 41700 dbu = 41.7 um and height 33800 dbu = 33.8 um, so the area is 1409.46 square microns. Dividing the product of dbu by 1000 once, not 1000 squared, is the classic error.

problems.q: A DEF file declares `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 ;` and `DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 60600 44500 ) ;`. What is the die area in square microns? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Width is 60600 dbu = 60.6 um and height 44500 dbu = 44.5 um, so the area is 2696.7 square microns. Dividing the product of dbu by 1000 once, not 1000 squared, is the classic error.

problems.q: A LEF SITE has width 0.19 um. A DEF with `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 4000 ;` places a row at x = 12920 with `DO 154 BY 1` and a STEP equal to the site width. What is the x coordinate, in DEF database units, of the right edge of the row?
problems.e: LEF dimensions are microns, DEF integers: the step is 0.19 × 4000 = 760 dbu, and the row ends at 12920 + 154 × 760 = 129960.

problems.q: A LEF SITE has width 0.19 um. A DEF with `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 2000 ;` places a row at x = 8360 with `DO 385 BY 1` and a STEP equal to the site width. What is the x coordinate, in DEF database units, of the right edge of the row?
problems.e: LEF dimensions are microns, DEF integers: the step is 0.19 × 2000 = 380 dbu, and the row ends at 8360 + 385 × 380 = 154660.

problems.q: A LEF SITE has width 0.2 um. A DEF with `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 4000 ;` places a row at x = 4000 with `DO 384 BY 1` and a STEP equal to the site width. What is the x coordinate, in DEF database units, of the right edge of the row?
problems.e: LEF dimensions are microns, DEF integers: the step is 0.2 × 4000 = 800 dbu, and the row ends at 4000 + 384 × 800 = 311200.

label: SDC as Tcl
lesson:
# SDC as Tcl

Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) is the language of timing intent: clocks, input and output delays, exceptions. It is not a standalone grammar but a set of Tcl commands, so an SDC file is a Tcl program. A tool that reads SDC must evaluate Tcl and must resolve object queries against its own database. Knowing this explains how constraints work, and how they silently break.

## SDC is a Tcl dialect

Each SDC line is a Tcl command: `create_clock -name clk -period 2.5 [get_ports clk]`. Tcl rules apply. Square brackets are command substitution: `get_ports clk` runs first and its result becomes an argument. A dollar sign before a name substitutes the variable's value, so `set p 2.5` followed by a reference to p after -period is legal. Braces quote literally, so `{in_a in_b}` is one word holding a two-element list. Loops, procedures and expressions are all available: a foreach loop over {a b c} whose body calls set_load on get_ports of the loop variable issues three constraints. A tool that only pattern-matches SDC lines will misread any file that uses these features, which is why real readers embed a Tcl interpreter and define the SDC commands inside it.

## Object queries return collections

Commands such as `get_ports`, `get_pins`, `get_cells`, `get_nets` and `get_clocks` look up database objects by name pattern and return a collection of object handles, not strings. `get_pins u1/*` returns every pin of u1. The constraint command then attaches to those objects. Two consequences follow. A pattern that matches nothing returns an empty collection, and the constraint silently applies to nothing, so careful tools warn on empty matches. And constraints bind through names: if synthesis renames `u_alu/add_0` to `u_alu/add_0_inst`, a constraint written against the old hierarchical name stops matching. Collections exist because re-resolving names for every command would be slow and ambiguous when a port and a net share a name.

## Interpreting SDC inside a tool

SDC numbers are unitless. `set_input_delay 300 -clock clk [get_ports a]` means 300 of whatever time unit is in effect, set by `set_units` or inherited from the library, so a file written for picoseconds and read in nanoseconds is off by a thousand. Tools differ in how much Tcl they allow. OpenSTA defines the SDC commands in its own Tcl interpreter and sources the file. Some sign-off flows use restricted readers that reject arbitrary Tcl, so that a constraint file cannot run side effects and means the same in every tool. Writing SDC back out after optimization is the reverse problem: collections of handles must be turned into names that resolve in the modified netlist.

## Going deeper

The SDC specification published with the open-source SDC parser; the OpenSTA documentation for read_sdc; Gangadharan and Churiwala, "Constraining Designs for Synthesis and Timing Analysis" (2013).

problems.q:
An SDC file contains a Tcl foreach loop over the list {a b c} whose body calls set_load 0.01 on get_ports of the loop variable. What does the tool see?

A) Three set_load commands, one per port

B) One set_load applied to a port named {a b c}

C) A syntax error, since loops are not SDC

D) One set_load on a port named after the variable
problems.a: Three set_load commands, one per port
problems.e: Because SDC is evaluated by a Tcl interpreter, the loop runs and the loop variable is substituted on each iteration.

problems.q:
Which value does `[get_ports clk]` do in `create_clock -period 2 [get_ports clk]`?

A) Runs get_ports first and passes its result as an argument

B) Comments out the port name

C) Groups the arguments into a list without evaluating

D) Declares a new port named clk
problems.a: Runs get_ports first and passes its result as an argument
problems.e: Square brackets are Tcl command substitution: the inner command runs and its result replaces the bracketed text.

problems.q:
An SDC file contains a Tcl foreach loop over the list {a b c} whose body calls set_load 0.01 on get_ports of the loop variable. What does the tool see?

A) A syntax error, since loops are not SDC

B) One set_load applied to a port named {a b c}

C) Three set_load commands, one per port

D) One set_load on a port named after the variable
problems.a: Three set_load commands, one per port
problems.e: Because SDC is evaluated by a Tcl interpreter, the loop runs and the loop variable is substituted on each iteration.

problems.q:
A constraint names `[get_pins u_core/u_alu/add_0/A]`, but synthesis renamed the instance. What is the likely outcome?

A) The tool finds the pin by its function

B) The query returns an empty collection and the constraint is lost

C) The design fails to link

D) The constraint moves to the nearest pin
problems.a: The query returns an empty collection and the constraint is lost
problems.e: Constraints bind to objects through names. When netlists are renamed, constraints written against hierarchical names silently stop matching.

problems.q:
`get_ports data*` matches nothing because the design's ports are named din[0] to din[7]. What does a careful tool do?

A) Warn that the pattern matched no objects, so the constraint applies to nothing

B) Apply the constraint to all ports

C) Silently match the closest names

D) Create ports named data*
problems.a: Warn that the pattern matched no objects, so the constraint applies to nothing
problems.e: A pattern that matches nothing silently drops a constraint. Tools warn because unconstrained paths are a classic source of escapes.

problems.q:
`get_ports data*` matches nothing because the design's ports are named din[0] to din[7]. What does a careful tool do?

A) Warn that the pattern matched no objects, so the constraint applies to nothing

B) Silently match the closest names

C) Apply the constraint to all ports

D) Create ports named data*
problems.a: Warn that the pattern matched no objects, so the constraint applies to nothing
problems.e: A pattern that matches nothing silently drops a constraint. Tools warn because unconstrained paths are a classic source of escapes.

problems.q:
An SDC file says `set_input_delay 300 -clock clk [get_ports a]` with no units. How does a tool interpret 300?

A) Always in nanoseconds

B) In the time unit in effect, from set_units or the library, so 300 is wrong if the unit is ns

C) Always in picoseconds

D) In clock periods of clk
problems.a: In the time unit in effect, from set_units or the library, so 300 is wrong if the unit is ns
problems.e: SDC numbers are unitless; their meaning comes from set_units or the library's time unit. 300 ns where 300 ps was meant is a classic constraint bug.

problems.q:
A tool writes constraints back out after optimization. What must write_sdc do with collections such as `[get_pins u1/*]`?

A) Write the matching objects by name in a form that resolves in the new netlist

B) Drop every constraint that used a wildcard

C) Write the pattern unchanged, whatever the netlist became

D) Write object handles as memory addresses
problems.a: Write the matching objects by name in a form that resolves in the new netlist
problems.e: Handles do not survive a session. Written constraints must name objects so that the next tool's queries find them.

problems.q:
A tool writes constraints back out after optimization. What must write_sdc do with collections such as `[get_pins u1/*]`?

A) Drop every constraint that used a wildcard

B) Write the pattern unchanged, whatever the netlist became

C) Write object handles as memory addresses

D) Write the matching objects by name in a form that resolves in the new netlist
problems.a: Write the matching objects by name in a form that resolves in the new netlist
problems.e: Handles do not survive a session. Written constraints must name objects so that the next tool's queries find them.

label: Parsing SPEF
lesson:
# Parsing SPEF

SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) carries the resistances and capacitances extracted from routed wires, net by net. Timers read it to compute wire delays, and it is often the largest file in the flow. A parser must handle the name map that compresses it, the unit header that gives its numbers meaning, and the per-net sections whose RC networks feed delay calculation.

## The name map compresses names

Hierarchical net names are long, and each appears many times in a SPEF: in the *D_NET line, in *CONN entries and in every node name of its RC network. The *NAME_MAP section assigns each name an index such as `*1234`, written once, and the body uses the index. Take the name u_core/u_alu/n_4521 (19 characters) appearing 12 times. Without the map that costs $12 \times 19 = 228$ bytes. With the map, references cost $12 \times 5 = 60$ bytes for the token *1234, and the map line costs $5 + 1 + 19 + 1 = 26$ bytes (index, space, name, newline), so the map saves $228 - 60 - 26 = 142$ bytes. A parser reads the map into a hash table first and resolves every token through it.

## Total capacitance of a D_NET

The header declares units: `*C_UNIT 1 PF`, `*R_UNIT 1 OHM`, `*T_UNIT 1 NS`. Each net section starts `*D_NET n17 <total cap>` followed by *CONN, *CAP and *RES. In *CAP, a line with one node is capacitance to ground, such as `1 n17:1 0.0012`; a line with two nodes is coupling capacitance, such as `3 n17:2 n940:1 0.0004`. The total on the *D_NET line includes both. With entries 0.0012, 0.0008 and coupling 0.0004 in pF, the total is $1.2 + 0.8 + 0.4 = 2.4$ fF. A coupling entry appears in each of the two nets' sections, so it counts toward each net's own total, and a crosstalk-aware timer keeps it as a coupling element rather than grounding it.

## Resistance along a parasitic path

The *RES section lists resistors as (index, node, node, value). Nodes are pins such as u1:ZN or internal points such as n17:3. The network is usually a tree rooted at the driver. With `*R_UNIT 1 KOHM`, the chain u1:ZN to n17:1 (0.012), n17:1 to n17:2 (0.030), n17:2 to u4:A (0.018), plus a branch n17:1 to u7:B (0.025), gives a driver-to-u4:A resistance of $12 + 30 + 18 = 60$ ohms; the branch to u7:B is not on that path. The parser builds an adjacency list over the nodes, then a delay calculator walks it, for example for Elmore delay. Lines can arrive in any order, so a reader must build the graph before walking it, and should flag loops or disconnected nodes.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1481 (the SPEF chapter); the OpenSTA source for its SPEF reader; the OpenRCX documentation in OpenROAD.

problems.q: A SPEF writer can replace the net name u_core/u_lsu/n_16735 (20 characters) by the index *18351 through *NAME_MAP. The name appears 14 times in the file. Each name-map line is the index, a space, the name and a newline. How many bytes does the map save?
problems.e: Without the map the name costs 14 × 20 = 280 bytes. With it, references cost 14 × 6 = 84 and the map line costs 6 + 1 + 20 + 1 = 28, so the saving is 168 bytes.

problems.q: A SPEF writer can replace the net name u_core/u_regfile/n_82940 (24 characters) by the index *79466 through *NAME_MAP. The name appears 17 times in the file. Each name-map line is the index, a space, the name and a newline. How many bytes does the map save?
problems.e: Without the map the name costs 17 × 24 = 408 bytes. With it, references cost 17 × 6 = 102 and the map line costs 6 + 1 + 24 + 1 = 32, so the saving is 274 bytes.

problems.q: A SPEF writer can replace the net name u_dsp/u_regfile/n_15089 (23 characters) by the index *83924 through *NAME_MAP. The name appears 24 times in the file. Each name-map line is the index, a space, the name and a newline. How many bytes does the map save?
problems.e: Without the map the name costs 24 × 23 = 552 bytes. With it, references cost 24 × 6 = 144 and the map line costs 6 + 1 + 23 + 1 = 31, so the saving is 377 bytes.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*C_UNIT 1 FF`. The *CAP section of `*D_NET n643` lists: 1 n643:1 4.8; 2 n643:2 4.8; 3 n643:3 4.4; 4 n643:3 n1831:2 0.9; 5 n643:3 n1473:2 0.2. Lines with one node are capacitance to ground and lines with two nodes are coupling capacitance. What total capacitance, in fF, should the *D_NET header carry for this net? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The total includes ground and coupling entries: 14 fF to ground plus 1.1 fF of coupling, scaled by the C unit (1 fF), is 15.1 fF.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*C_UNIT 1 FF`. The *CAP section of `*D_NET n40` lists: 1 n40:1 4.5; 2 n40:2 5.9; 3 n40:3 3.5; 4 n40:1 n1039:4 1.6; 5 n40:1 n1516:2 0.1. Lines with one node are capacitance to ground and lines with two nodes are coupling capacitance. What total capacitance, in fF, should the *D_NET header carry for this net? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The total includes ground and coupling entries: 13.9 fF to ground plus 1.7 fF of coupling, scaled by the C unit (1 fF), is 15.6 fF.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*C_UNIT 1 PF`. The *CAP section of `*D_NET n200` lists: 1 n200:1 0.0035; 2 n200:2 0.0053; 3 n200:3 0.0055; 4 n200:4 0.0028; 5 n200:5 0.0049; 6 n200:3 n1761:4 0.0006; 7 n200:5 n1363:1 0.0018; 8 n200:3 n1895:1 0.0008. Lines with one node are capacitance to ground and lines with two nodes are coupling capacitance. What total capacitance, in fF, should the *D_NET header carry for this net? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The total includes ground and coupling entries: 22 fF to ground plus 3.2 fF of coupling, scaled by the C unit (1000 fF), is 25.2 fF.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*R_UNIT 1 OHM`. The *RES section of `*D_NET n489`, driven by u1:ZN, lists (index, node, node, value): 1 u1:ZN n489:1 83; 3 n489:2 u4:A 26; 4 n489:1 u7:B 51; 2 n489:1 n489:2 60. What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?
problems.e: Follow the chain u1:ZN through n489:1 ... n489:2 to u4:A, skipping the branch to u7:B, and scale by the R unit: 169 ohms.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*R_UNIT 1 KOHM`. The *RES section of `*D_NET n104`, driven by u1:ZN, lists (index, node, node, value): 3 n104:2 u4:A 0.048; 1 u1:ZN n104:1 0.013; 2 n104:1 n104:2 0.034; 4 n104:2 u7:B 0.068. What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?
problems.e: Follow the chain u1:ZN through n104:1 ... n104:2 to u4:A, skipping the branch to u7:B, and scale by the R unit: 95 ohms.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*R_UNIT 1 OHM`. The *RES section of `*D_NET n560`, driven by u1:ZN, lists (index, node, node, value): 5 n560:4 n560:5 12; 2 n560:1 n560:2 49; 1 u1:ZN n560:1 87; 6 n560:5 u4:A 20; 3 n560:2 n560:3 14; 7 n560:4 u7:B 84; 4 n560:3 n560:4 38. What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?
problems.e: Follow the chain u1:ZN through n560:1 ... n560:5 to u4:A, skipping the branch to u7:B, and scale by the R unit: 220 ohms.

label: GDSII stream records
lesson:
# GDSII stream records

GDSII is the binary stream format in which layouts reach the mask shop, and KLayout, Magic and every DRC engine read and write it. Unlike LEF and DEF it is a flat sequence of typed binary records, so a reader is a loop over record headers. Knowing the record layout lets a tool designer size files, write a minimal reader, and convert stored integers into physical coordinates.

## Record headers and the XY record

Every GDSII record starts with a 4-byte header: a 2-byte big-endian length that counts the whole record including the header, a 1-byte record type (HEADER, BGNLIB, UNITS, BGNSTR, BOUNDARY, XY, ENDEL and so on) and a 1-byte data type (no data, 2-byte integer, 4-byte integer, 8-byte real, ASCII string). A reader reads the header, then length minus 4 bytes of payload, and dispatches on the type. Coordinates live in XY records as pairs of 4-byte signed integers, 8 bytes per point. A BOUNDARY is closed by repeating its first point, so a rectangle with 4 vertices stores 5 points: $4 + 8 \times 5 = 44$ bytes. An L-shaped polygon with 6 vertices stores 7 points, $4 + 56 = 60$ bytes.

## Bytes in a layout element

An element is a sequence of records ending in ENDEL. A BOUNDARY element is BOUNDARY (4 bytes, no data), LAYER (4 + 2), DATATYPE (4 + 2), XY (4 + 8(n + 1)) and ENDEL (4), so an n-vertex boundary costs $24 + 8(n + 1)$ bytes: 64 bytes for a rectangle. A PATH element is a wire with a centerline: PATH, LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (4 + 4, a 4-byte integer), the XY of its k points (not closed, so no repeated point) and ENDEL, which is $28 + 8k$ bytes. A structure holding two rectangles and a 3-point path is $64 + 64 + 52 = 180$ bytes. Sizes like these explain why flat GDS of a large chip runs to many gigabytes, and why hierarchy, with SREF and AREF references to shared structures, and the more compact OASIS format matter.

## Database units to microns

Coordinates are integers in database units. The UNITS record holds two 8-byte reals: the size of a database unit in user units, and its size in meters. A typical library stores 0.001 and 1e-9: one database unit is 1 nm, and the user unit is the micron. An XY integer of 123456 is then $123456 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 123.456$ um. With a database unit of 5e-10 m the same integer is 61.728 um. A reader must use the meter value, not assume nanometers, and a tool that merges GDS files from different sources, as the final step of a flow merges cell GDS into the design, must rescale any file whose database unit differs, or reject it. The 8-byte reals use the GDSII excess-64 base-16 floating-point format, not IEEE 754, which a hand-written reader must decode explicitly.

## Going deeper

The GDSII Stream Format manual (Calma, release 6.0); the KLayout documentation on stream formats.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a polygon with 10 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 10 + 1 = 11 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 11 = 92 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a polygon with 10 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 10 + 1 = 11 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 11 = 92 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a U-shaped polygon with 8 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 8 + 1 = 9 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 9 = 76 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A structure holds a 6-vertex boundary and a 8-vertex boundary. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 80 + 96, totalling 176 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A PATH is PATH (4 bytes), LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (header plus a 4-byte integer), XY with its points (an open path does not repeat a point) and ENDEL. A structure holds a 8-vertex boundary, a 4-vertex boundary and a 4-point PATH with a WIDTH record. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 96 + 64 + 64, totalling 224 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A PATH is PATH (4 bytes), LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (header plus a 4-byte integer), XY with its points (an open path does not repeat a point) and ENDEL. A structure holds a 4-vertex boundary, a 8-vertex boundary, a 6-vertex boundary, a 6-vertex boundary and a 2-point PATH with a WIDTH record. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 64 + 96 + 80 + 80 + 48, totalling 368 bytes.

problems.e: One database unit is 1e-9 m = 0.001 um, so 302169 units are 302.169 um.

problems.q: A GDSII library's UNITS record holds the size of a database unit in user units, 0.01, and in meters, 1e-8. An XY coordinate stores the integer 659357. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: One database unit is 1e-8 m = 0.01 um, so 659357 units are 6593.57 um.

problems.q: A GDSII library's UNITS record holds the size of a database unit in user units, 0.0005, and in meters, 5e-10. An XY coordinate stores the integer 1839518. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: One database unit is 5e-10 m = 0.0005 um, so 1839518 units are 919.759 um.

label: EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards
prereqs: The map of design representations and formats
lesson:
# EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards

Beyond Verilog, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SPEF and GDS, a tool meets a set of interchange standards for netlists, IP metadata and power intent. Each comes with its own syntax and its own parsing strategy: S-expressions, XML with a schema, or Tcl. Consortia such as Si2 steward several of them. A tool designer should recognize each format, know what it carries, and know what reader it needs.

## EDIF netlist interchange

EDIF (Electronic Design Interchange Format) describes netlists as nested S-expressions, LISP-style parenthesized lists: libraries contain cells, cells contain views, views have an interface (ports) and contents (instances and nets). One recursive reader can parse any EDIF file, because every construct is a list whose first element is a keyword. The price is verbosity: keywords repeat for every object. EDIF remains common in FPGA flows and older tool hand-offs. The parser's job is the same as for a Verilog netlist: build the same instances, nets and terminals in the object model. Importing the same design from EDIF and from Verilog should give identical connectivity, which is a cheap and powerful regression test for both readers.

## IP-XACT component metadata

IP-XACT (IEEE 1685) is an XML schema for describing IP blocks: components, bus interfaces with their port mappings, memory maps, address blocks and registers with their fields. It does not describe logic. It is the single source from which tools generate register RTL, C header files and documentation, and from which SoC integration tools wire blocks together by matching bus interfaces. A reader uses a standard XML parser and validates against the schema, rather than a hand-written grammar. A register of 32 bits with fields at bit offsets 0, 8 and 16 generates both the decode logic and the software mask constants, so hardware and software cannot drift apart.

## UPF power intent and the Si2 coalitions

UPF (Unified Power Format, IEEE 1801) captures power intent outside the RTL: `create_power_domain`, supply nets and ports, isolation, level shifting, retention and power states. Like SDC it is Tcl, so a tool reads it with a Tcl interpreter that defines these commands, and keeping it separate lets one RTL be implemented under different power strategies. Si2 (Silicon Integration Initiative) is an industry consortium whose member coalitions maintain standards, among them OpenAccess, a design database API, and the reference LEF/DEF parsers on which OpenDB's readers are based. Shared reference parsers matter because a format is only as standard as its corner cases: when tools share a parser, the same file means the same design to each of them.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1685 (IP-XACT); IEEE Std 1801 (UPF); the EDIF 2 0 0 specification; the Si2 OpenAccess documentation.

label: One database, many engines
prereqs: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
lesson:
# One database, many engines

An EDA flow chains engines: floorplanner, placer, clock-tree builder, router, extractor, timer. They can be separate programs exchanging files, or modules of one program sharing one in-memory design database, as in OpenROAD. The choice shapes everything else: speed of optimization loops, how engines learn of each other's edits, and what can go wrong when they share state. Tool designers must know both architectures and their costs.

## Point tools that exchange files

In the classic architecture each step is a separate program. The placer writes DEF; the router reads it and writes routed DEF; the extractor writes SPEF; the timer reads Verilog, DEF, SPEF, Liberty and SDC. The formats are the contract, so any tool can be swapped for another vendor's. The cost is serialization at every boundary: a design with ten million instances may take minutes to write and parse, so a loop that wants timing feedback after every few thousand moves is impractical. A second cost is loss: anything the format cannot express, such as a tool-specific attribute, disappears in the round trip unless both sides agree on an extension.

## Engines on one in-memory database

OpenROAD links its engines into one application around OpenDB. Floorplanning, placement, resizing, CTS, routing, extraction and timing read and edit the same objects, so an engine's results are visible to the next immediately, with no file in between. This is what makes tight loops possible: the resizer swaps a master, the timer updates incrementally, and the resizer asks again, thousands of times. Each engine still keeps its own derived structures, such as the timer's graph with arrival times or the router's grid, built from the database. So sharing data creates a new duty: when one engine edits the database, every engine caching derived results must hear about it, typically through callbacks, and update incrementally.

## Consistency when engines share state

Shared mutable state brings classic hazards. If two engines edit concurrently without coordination, one can read a half-applied edit or corrupt a shared list, so tools allow one writer at a time, partition the design into regions, or use transactions. If the router deletes a wire while the timer holds a raw pointer to it, the timer crashes later; stable ids or handles, plus deletion callbacks, avoid that. Every path into the database must notify, including user Tcl edits; otherwise a manual change leaves the timer's cache stale and its next report wrong. Files do not disappear: shared-database tools still write DEF, Verilog and SPEF at stage boundaries as checkpoints and for hand-off to sign-off tools.

## Going deeper

Ajayi et al., "OpenROAD: Toward a Self-Driving, Open-Source Digital Layout Implementation Tool Chain" (GOMACTech 2019); the OpenROAD developer guide; the OpenDB documentation.

A) DEF cannot store placement

B) Files force every tool to use the same algorithm

C) Point tools cannot share a Liberty file

D) Every step re-parses and rebuilds the whole design, so small loops are slow
problems.a: Every step re-parses and rebuilds the whole design, so small loops are slow
problems.e: Writing and parsing gigabytes of text at every hand-off makes tight optimize-and-analyze loops impractical.

label: Plug-in architectures
lesson:
# Plug-in architectures

Every long-lived EDA tool grows by extension: new synthesis passes, new placement penalties, new reports, new readers. A plug-in architecture lets that growth happen without editing the core. The patterns are old and simple, a registry, a factory and an interface, but the hard parts are the boundary itself: how plug-ins are built and loaded, and how the contract between host and plug-in survives change.

## Registries and factories

A registry maps a name to a way of constructing an implementation. Yosys shows the pattern: a pass is a C++ class derived from `Pass`, its constructor passes a name such as "my_opt" to the base class, and one static instance of the class is declared. Constructing that instance at start-up adds it to a global name-to-pass map, so typing `my_opt` in the shell finds and runs it. The same pattern serves policies inside an engine: a placer defines an abstract density-penalty interface, implementations register under names such as "bell", and a config file selects one by name. The core calls only the interface. Adding a penalty adds a registration, not a core edit. Duplicate names should be rejected, since silent replacement makes behavior depend on load order.

## Compiled-in modules versus loaded libraries

A plug-in can be compiled into the binary or loaded at run time. Yosys supports both: built-in passes, and shared libraries loaded with `yosys -m my_plugin.so`, whose static objects register their passes when the library loads. OpenROAD compiles its tools into one application, each module adding its Tcl commands at start-up. Compiled-in modules are built together, so they agree on the database layout, compiler and standard library; the price is a rebuild to add one. Loaded libraries can be added by users, but a C++ object crossing a library boundary depends on the C++ ABI: class layout, name mangling, standard-library types and exceptions. A plug-in built with another compiler version can compile cleanly and crash. A C-callable boundary passing plain structs and opaque handles is the robust choice.

## Versioning the plug-in contract

Once published, a plug-in interface is a promise. If the host adds a field in the middle of a struct, old plug-ins read wrong offsets. The defenses are standard: every struct carries a version or size field, fields are only appended, the plug-in declares the interface version it was built against, and the host checks it at load time so a mismatch is a clear error rather than a later crash. Plug-ins should keep no hidden global state, so instances run independently on many designs in parallel and results do not depend on scheduling. And the interface stays narrow: every function exposed is a function the core can never change freely again, so hosts expose a small, stable seam rather than their internals.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual chapter on writing extensions; the OpenROAD developer guide on adding a tool; Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), on Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

problems.q:
Two plug-ins both register under the name "route_cost". What should the registry do?

A) Merge their code

B) Rename the second one at random

C) Refuse the duplicate or report it, rather than silently replacing one

D) Keep both and pick randomly
problems.a: Refuse the duplicate or report it, rather than silently replacing one
problems.e: Silent replacement makes behavior depend on load order, which is a nondeterminism bug.

problems.q:
A Yosys pass is a C++ class whose constructor passes the name "my_opt" to the Pass base class, and one static instance is declared. How does `my_opt` become a command?

A) The user edits Yosys's main function

B) Yosys parses the C++ source at run time

C) The static instance registers itself by name in a global registry at start-up

D) The pass is found by scanning the file system
problems.a: The static instance registers itself by name in a global registry at start-up
problems.e: Self-registering objects are the classic plug-in pattern: constructing the instance adds it to a name-to-object map that the shell looks up.

problems.q:
Two plug-ins both register under the name "route_cost". What should the registry do?

A) Refuse the duplicate or report it, rather than silently replacing one

B) Rename the second one at random

C) Keep both and pick randomly

D) Merge their code
problems.a: Refuse the duplicate or report it, rather than silently replacing one
problems.e: Silent replacement makes behavior depend on load order, which is a nondeterminism bug.

problems.q:
Yosys can load an extension with `yosys -m my_plugin.so`. What kind of plug-in is that?

A) A pass compiled into the Yosys binary

B) A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes

C) A Verilog module synthesized by Yosys

D) A Tcl script interpreted by Yosys
problems.a: A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes
problems.e: Dynamic loading lets users add passes without rebuilding Yosys; the loaded library's static objects register themselves.

problems.q:
Which plug-in boundary is the most robust to compiler differences between host and plug-in?

A) Passing C++ exceptions across the boundary

B) Sharing class hierarchies with virtual inheritance

C) Passing std::map objects by reference

D) A C-callable interface passing plain structs and opaque handles
problems.a: A C-callable interface passing plain structs and opaque handles
problems.e: The C ABI is stable across compilers; standard-library types and exceptions are not.

problems.q:
A plug-in built with one compiler version crashes inside a host built with another, though both compile cleanly. What is the likely cause?

A) The host's Tcl version is too new

B) The design is too large

C) The C++ ABI (layout, name mangling, standard-library types) differs across the boundary

D) The plug-in has a syntax error
problems.a: The C++ ABI (layout, name mangling, standard-library types) differs across the boundary
problems.e: C++ objects crossing a dynamic-library boundary must agree on layout and runtime. A C interface or a pinned toolchain avoids this.

problems.q:
A plug-in asks the host for an API version it does not provide. When should the host find out?

A) At the end of the flow

B) At load time, by checking the plug-in's declared interface version

C) Never; versions are advisory

D) When the plug-in first crashes
problems.a: At load time, by checking the plug-in's declared interface version
problems.e: Checking a declared version at load turns a late, confusing crash into an immediate, clear error.

problems.q:
A host adds a field to the struct it passes to plug-ins. Old plug-ins now read the wrong offsets. What prevents this?

A) Making all fields private

B) Renaming the struct

C) A version or size field in the struct, and adding fields only at the end

D) Recompiling the host only
problems.a: A version or size field in the struct, and adding fields only at the end
problems.e: Versioned, append-only structs let old plug-ins keep working and let the host detect what each plug-in understands.

problems.q:
A plug-in keeps hidden global state between calls. Why does that hurt a host that runs it on many designs in parallel?

A) It prevents the host from loading the plug-in

B) Calls interfere through the shared state, so results depend on scheduling

C) Global state is forbidden by C++

D) It makes the plug-in compile slower
problems.a: Calls interfere through the shared state, so results depend on scheduling
problems.e: Plug-ins should take their state as explicit arguments so instances are independent and results reproducible.

label: Database callbacks and observers
lesson:
# Database callbacks and observers

When engines share one design database, an engine that caches derived data, a timer's arrival times or a placer's density map, must learn when the design changes. The observer pattern does this: engines register callbacks with the database, and every edit notifies the subscribers. OpenDB provides this through callback objects attached to a block. The design questions are how many notifications an edit stream generates and how to keep their cost low.

## Observers subscribe to edit events

An observer registers for the kinds of edit it cares about. A timer cares about master swaps and pin connections, because both change delays and topology; a density map cares about moves and new instances; a global router cares about moves and connections. On each edit the database calls every observer subscribed to that kind. With a timer on {swap, connect}, a density map on {move, create} and a router on {move, connect}, the edit stream move, swap, connect, move costs $2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7$ callbacks. Subscribing only to relevant kinds matters: an engine that subscribes to everything pays for every edit in the flow, and a million-move detailed placement then makes millions of useless calls.

## Mark dirty, recompute on query

A callback should be cheap. Recomputing timing inside every callback is ruinous when an optimizer makes thousands of edits between questions. Instead the observer records what changed, often just a dirty flag or a set of dirty objects, and recomputes when someone asks. For the session swap, move, swap, QUERY, connect, QUERY, QUERY with a timer subscribed to swap and connect, an eager timer recomputes 3 times, once per relevant edit. A lazy one recomputes at the first query (dirty from the two swaps), at the second (dirty from the connect), and not at the third (still clean): 2 times. The edits between queries are merged into one update, which is how incremental timers stay fast inside optimization loops.

## Batching notifications per transaction

Even cheap callbacks cost a function call and often a lock per edit. A database can batch: edits inside a transaction are collected, and at commit each observer that subscribed to at least one of them gets a single call carrying the list. With three transactions, if the timer is touched in all three and the density map in two, the batched cost is 5 calls, however many edits each transaction held. Batching also gives observers a consistent view: they never see a half-applied change such as an instance moved but not yet reconnected. The trade-off is latency, since an observer learns of an edit only at commit, and memory for the pending edit list.

## Going deeper

The OpenDB documentation on dbBlockCallBackObj; Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), the Observer pattern.

problems.q: A design database notifies registered observers on every edit: the power analyzer subscribes to master swapped and pin connected or disconnected; the density map subscribes to instance moved; the global router subscribes to instance moved and instance created; the timer subscribes to instance moved, master swapped and instance created. An optimizer then makes these edits in order: instance moved, instance created, pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, master swapped. How many callback invocations does the database make in total?
problems.e: Each edit calls every observer subscribed to its kind: 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2, which sums to 10.

problems.q: A design database notifies registered observers on every edit: the timer subscribes to instance moved and instance created; the power analyzer subscribes to instance moved; the global router subscribes to instance created. An optimizer then makes these edits in order: instance created, instance created, instance created, instance moved, pin connected or disconnected. label: Incremental computation and dependency graphs
lesson:
# Incremental computation and dependency graphs

Every EDA tool caches derived results: parasitics computed from wires, delays from parasitics, arrivals from delays, slacks from arrivals. When the design changes, recomputing everything is too slow, and recomputing too little gives wrong answers. A dependency graph makes the cache honest. Each derived result is a node, each edge says which input it was computed from, and an edit tells the tool exactly which cached values may now be stale. This structure sits underneath incremental timing, incremental legalization and incremental builds alike.

## Invalidation follows forward edges

Draw an edge $u \to v$ whenever result $v$ is computed from $u$. The graph is acyclic, because no result can depend on itself, so it has a topological order. When an edit modifies node $u$, every node reachable from $u$ along edges may be stale, and no other node can be: its inputs are untouched. The invalid set is therefore the forward reachable set of the edited nodes, found by one depth-first or breadth-first search.

Example: edges $A \to B$, $A \to C$, $B \to D$, $C \to D$, $D \to E$ and $F \to E$. An edit to $B$ invalidates $D$ and $E$, two results; $A$, $C$ and $F$ keep their cached values. With several edits, the invalid set is the union of their reachable sets, so a result reachable from two edits is invalidated once, not twice.

## A query needs only its dirty ancestors

Invalidation is cheap; recomputation is the expensive part, and a lazy tool postpones it until someone asks. A query for node $q$ must bring $q$ up to date, and that requires every input of $q$ to be valid first, recursively. So the work for one query is the set of dirty nodes that are $q$ itself or ancestors of $q$. Dirty nodes elsewhere stay dirty.

Continuing the example, edit $B$ and then query $D$. The dirty set is $\{D, E\}$. The ancestors of $D$ are $A$, $B$ and $C$, all clean, so only $D$ is recomputed: one evaluation, although two results are dirty. A query for $E$ would recompute $D$ and then $E$. This is why a timer asked for the slack of one endpoint touches only that endpoint's fanin cone.

## Recompute in levels

When everything dirty must be refreshed, the topological order says what may run together. Give each dirty node a level: one more than the highest level among its dirty inputs, and 1 if all its inputs are clean. Nodes on the same level do not depend on one another, so a parallel engine can recompute a whole level at once, and the number of rounds equals the deepest level.

Example: edit $A$ in the graph above. Dirty nodes are $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$. $B$ and $C$ have only the clean input $A$, so both are level 1. $D$ depends on $B$ and $C$, so level 2. $E$ depends on $D$ and the clean $F$, so level 3. Three rounds, the longest dirty path, however many workers there are. Long dependency chains limit incremental parallelism just as they limit full recomputation.

## Going deeper
